questions.q: What genuine, scientifically meaningful milestone have multiple hardware platforms demonstrated regarding logical qubits?
options: That an encoded logical qubit's error rate can be made lower than the error rate of its best individual physical qubit
That a fully fault-tolerant, million-qubit quantum computer has been built
That classical error correction has been proven impossible
That the threshold theorem has been experimentally disproven
questions.explain: Showing a logical qubit outperforming its best constituent physical qubit is real experimental evidence that redundancy plus correct syndrome extraction and correction can net out to better reliability -- a genuine, nontrivial milestone.

questions.q: Why are multiple different qubit hardware platforms (superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral-atom, photonic) being pursued in parallel?
options: There is genuine scientific uncertainty about which platform's tradeoffs will ultimately scale best toward fault tolerance
Only one platform is actually viable, and the others are purely for marketing purposes
All platforms are identical in every practical respect
Government regulations require multiple platforms to be researched simultaneously
questions.explain: Each platform has different tradeoffs (speed, coherence time, layout flexibility, decoherence channels), reflecting real, unresolved scientific and engineering uncertainty about the best path forward.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say current hardware demonstrations don't constitute fault-tolerant computing, even with the logical-error-rate milestone achieved?
options: Useful fault-tolerant computation needs hundreds to tens of millions of physical qubits per chapter 6's math, while current devices encode only a small number of logical qubits, far short of that scale
The logical-error-rate milestone was later found to be fraudulent
Fault-tolerant computing has actually already been achieved, contrary to the lesson's framing
NISQ-era hardware no longer exists as a category
questions.explain: The resource-estimation math from chapter 6 sets the real scale required; current small-scale demonstrations are necessary steps toward that, not evidence it has been reached.

questions.q: Why does the lesson deliberately avoid citing specific current qubit-count or fidelity records as settled facts?
options: Such numbers change quickly and would likely become stale or imprecise; the durable claim is the categorical gap between small-scale demonstrations and large-scale fault tolerance
No hardware platform has ever published any such numbers
Specific numbers are classified and cannot legally be discussed
The course considers all published hardware results to be fabricated
questions.explain: The lesson's honesty approach is to state the durable, categorical fact (demonstrations vs. what's needed) rather than a specific number that would likely be outdated by the time it's read.

questions.q: What is the 'categorical gap' the lesson draws between current demonstrations and real fault tolerance?
options: Small-scale, few-logical-qubit demonstrations versus large-scale, many-logical-qubit, continuously-operating systems needed for useful computation
There is no gap; the two categories are identical
The gap is only about which programming language is used to control the hardware
The gap is purely a difference in qubit color on a circuit diagram
questions.explain: The lesson frames the real distinction as one of scale and continuous operation, not just raw technical capability -- current demonstrations are real but categorically smaller than what useful fault tolerance requires.
